passage:
Daycare note, Toddler Room. Written by Rajni, caregiver.
Rehana (19 months) had a lovely moment today. A pigeon landed on the window ledge during snack time. I said, "Look, Rehana!" and turned my head towards it. She followed my eyes, spotted the bird and gasped. Then she pointed at it herself and looked back at me, checking that I had seen it too. We named it together: "Bird!" 🐦
Next step: I'll keep pointing out things around the room and wait for her to share her own finds.

qa.q: What landed on the window ledge during snack time?
qa.a: A pigeon landed on the window ledge.

qa.q: Why did Rehana look back at Rajni after pointing at the bird?
qa.a: She seemed to want to make sure Rajni was sharing the same exciting sight, enjoying it together.

qa.q: How could Rajni build on this at daycare?
qa.a: Rajni can keep pointing out interesting things and waiting for Rehana to point and share her own discoveries.

qa.q: What might it be like for Rajni when Rehana checks back with Rajni?
qa.a: It likely feels rewarding and warm, because the toddler is inviting Rajni into a shared moment.

grounding: It shows joint attention: a toddler following a caregiver's gaze and pointing to share focus.

passage:
Kunal carried Mridul on his hip along the edge of the mustard field. The yellow went on and on. Suddenly Kunal stopped and pointed at the neem tree. "Mridul, dekho! Mor!"
Mridul looked at his father's finger first, then followed it to the branch. A peacock was sitting there, its long tail hanging down. Mridul's mouth opened wide. He stretched his own arm out, pointed, and turned to his father's face.
"Haan, mor," Kunal said, smiling.
Mridul pointed again and bounced.

qa.q: Where was the peacock sitting?
qa.a: It was sitting on a branch of the neem tree.

qa.q: What does Mridul's bouncing and pointing again suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he is excited and wants his father to keep sharing the discovery with him.

qa.q: What could Kunal try on their next walk to help Mridul learn from shared looking?
qa.a: He could point to other animals or plants, name them, and pause so Mridul can point first.

qa.q: How does Kunal seem to experience this moment?
qa.a: He seems pleased and connected, answering Mridul's point with a smile and the word for peacock.

grounding: It shows a toddler following a caregiver's pointing to share focus on an object in a rural setting.

passage:
At the market in Kumasi, Bilal held Kwame's hand while they waited for the bread. A man walked past carrying a stack of bright woven baskets on his head. Bilal gasped softly and looked up at them. Kwame watched Bilal's face, then twisted round to see where he was looking. He spotted the baskets and laughed.
"Baskets," Bilal said.
Kwame lifted his arm and pointed. "Ba!" He turned back to check Bilal was still looking.
"Yes, big baskets!"

qa.q: What was the man carrying on his head?
qa.a: He was carrying a stack of bright woven baskets.

qa.q: How can you tell Kwame wanted to share the sight with Bilal?
qa.a: After pointing he turned back to check Bilal was still looking, which shows he was excited and wanted them to look together.

qa.q: How could Bilal support this kind of shared looking?
qa.a: He can keep naming what they both look at and answer Kwame's points with words, like "Yes, big baskets!"

qa.q: If you were Bilal, what might you notice about Kwame's growth?
qa.a: You might notice he now follows your gaze and points back, a sign he is learning by sharing attention.

grounding: It shows joint attention: a toddler following an adult's gaze and pointing to share focus.

passage: I'm Jyoti from next door. Yesterday I watched Sangeeta, who is fourteen months old, on her mother's lap. Her mother pointed to the parrot on the wire and said, "Look, tota!" Sangeeta turned, followed the finger, and found the bird. Then she looked back at her mother's face and squealed, as if checking, "You see it too?" Her mother laughed and nodded. I can't know what Sangeeta was thinking, but they seemed to share that parrot.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta's mother point to?
qa.a: She pointed to the parrot on the wire and said, "Look, tota!"

qa.q: Why might Sangeeta have looked back at her mother's face?
qa.a: She seemed excited and eager to share the moment, checking that her mother was seeing the same bird, though Jyoti cannot be sure.

qa.q: How could a caregiver build on moments like this?
qa.a: Point to interesting things, name them, and wait for the child to look and look back, then respond warmly to what she noticed.

qa.q: What is it like for Sangeeta's mother when Sangeeta squeals and looks back?
qa.a: She seems delighted, laughing and nodding, enjoying the shared moment with her daughter.

grounding: A neighbour observes a toddler following her mother's point to a bird and looking back to share focus.

passage:
Monday: Rajni pointed at a crow on the balcony. Kalyani, one year old, stared at Rajni's finger, not the crow.

Thursday: Rajni pointed again and said, "Kalyani, crow!" This time Kalyani's eyes slid along the finger and landed on the bird. "Ah!"

Two weeks later: A plane roared overhead. Kalyani pointed up herself, then twisted round to see Rajni's face. Rajni looked up. "Yes, plane!" Kalyani bounced, clapping.

qa.q: What did Kalyani look at on Monday when Rajni pointed?
qa.a: She stared at Rajni's finger, not the crow.

qa.q: How can you tell Kalyani wanted to share the plane with Rajni?
qa.a: Kalyani pointed up and twisted round to see Rajni's face, then bounced and clapped with delight when Rajni looked too.

qa.q: What small habit of Rajni's helped Kalyani learn?
qa.a: She kept pointing at things, naming them and following Kalyani's own pointing, giving her many chances to practise shared looking.

qa.q: What would change if Rajni had not looked up when Kalyani pointed?
qa.a: Kalyani would miss the shared moment, and she might point less often if no one responded 😔

grounding: Shows a toddler progressing over weeks from looking at a pointing finger to following and then starting a point herself.

passage:
On the balcony of their Mumbai flat, Manoj held fourteen-month-old Mridul on his hip.
“Look, Mridul! Kabootar!” He pointed at the pigeon on the railing.
Mridul looked at his father's finger first. Then his eyes followed the line to the pigeon. He went still. Then he turned back to his father's face, eyes wide, and stretched out his own hand towards the bird.
“Ba! Ba!”
“Yes, bird,” Manoj laughed. “You saw it too.”

qa.q: What did Manoj point at on the balcony?
qa.a: He pointed at the pigeon on the railing.

qa.q: What does Mridul's turning back to his father's face suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he was excited and curious and wanted to share the moment with his father.

qa.q: How could Manoj build on this moment?
qa.a: He could keep pointing out and naming things on their walks, waiting for Mridul to look and then responding warmly.

qa.q: What is it like for Manoj when Mridul looks back at him?
qa.a: He feels delighted and connected, knowing they are looking at the same thing together 🙂

grounding: A toddler follows his father's pointing to share attention on a pigeon.

passage:
“Devika, listen! What's that?”
A roaring sound filled the sky above their Pune colony. Vidya tilted her head back and looked up.
Eighteen-month-old Devika looked at her mother's face, then up where she was looking.
“There! Hawai jahaaz!” said Vidya, pointing.
Devika pointed too. “Da!”
“Yes, aeroplane! Going up, up, up.”
Devika turned to Nani on the steps. “Da! Da!”
“I see it, beta,” Nani said. “You showed me.”

qa.q: What sound filled the sky?
qa.a: A roaring sound filled the sky above their Pune colony.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when she turned to show Nani the aeroplane?
qa.a: She felt excited and eager to share her discovery with someone else.

qa.q: How could Vidya and Nani keep encouraging this kind of sharing?
qa.a: They could keep looking and pointing at interesting sights and respond warmly whenever Devika points things out.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when Devika points the plane out to her?
qa.a: She feels delighted and included, seeing the little girl share what she noticed.

grounding: A toddler follows her mother's gaze and pointing, then shares the focus with her grandmother.

passage:
Daycare note, Holi week. Teacher: Alka.
Today we put out small bowls of flower colour for the children to look at, not throw. Nandini, two, was busy with the blocks.
I said her name and looked at the yellow bowl. Nandini looked at my face, then followed my eyes to the bowl. She pointed at it and said, “Lelo!” (yellow). Then she looked back at me to check I'd seen.
Next step: more looking games with the colours tomorrow 🌼

qa.q: What was Nandini busy with before the teacher said her name?
qa.a: She was busy with the blocks.

qa.q: What does Nandini looking back at the teacher suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt curious and pleased, and wanted to check that they were sharing the same thing.

qa.q: Why are looking games a good next step?
qa.a: They give Nandini more chances to follow a caregiver's gaze and share focus, which builds shared learning.

qa.q: How might Alka feel seeing Nandini follow her eyes?
qa.a: Alka likely feels pleased and encouraged, noticing a small but important step in Nandini's development.

grounding: A daycare teacher notes a two-year-old following her gaze to share focus during Holi week.

passage: On Makar Sankranti in Idar, the sky over the fields was full of kites. Irawati held Siddharth, not yet two, on her hip. "Look, beta!" She pointed at a big red kite. He kept pointing at each new kite and checking her face.

qa.q: How does Irawati experience Siddharth pointing and looking back?
qa.a: She is happy and amused, sharing the moment with Siddharth.

passage: The first snow of winter was falling in Oslo. Ingrid knelt beside Javier's stroller. "Javier, look!" She pointed at a small red bird on a snowy branch. Javier, eighteen months, looked at her eyes first, then turned where her finger went. He saw the bird and gasped. He stretched out his own mitten, pointing. "Bah!" He looked back at Ingrid to see if she saw it too. "Yes, a bird," she whispered. They watched it together until it flew away.

qa.q: What was the bird sitting on?
qa.a: A snowy branch.

qa.q: What was Javier feeling when he gasped at the bird?
qa.a: He felt excited and delighted by the surprise of the bird.

qa.q: How did Ingrid help Javier share attention?
qa.a: She pointed, waited for him to find the bird, then named it quietly when he looked back.

qa.q: How might Ingrid feel when Javier looks back to check she saw it?
qa.a: She likely feels warm and connected, happy to share his discovery.

grounding: In the first snow, a toddler follows a caregiver's point to a bird and checks back to share it.

I can't know what he was thinking, but they seemed to be looking at the same thing together.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see Mohit and Dadi?
qa.a: Gurpreet sees them sharing a moment of attention, while unsure what Mohit was thinking.

passage:
Monsoon, first day: Avni pointed at the window. "Look, rain!" Irfan, fifteen months, stared at her face, not the window.
Four days later: Avni pointed again and said, "Rain, Irfan!" His eyes followed her finger to the glass. He squealed and slapped the pane.
Next week: Irfan pointed at a crow on the wet railing, then turned to check Avni was looking. She laughed. "Yes! A crow!" He grinned, pointing again and again.

qa.q: What did Irfan point at in the last beat?
qa.a: A crow on the wet railing.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel when Avni said "Yes! A crow!"?
qa.a: He felt delighted and pleased, grinning and pointing again and again.

qa.q: How can Avni keep building this shared attention?
qa.a: Keep pointing at interesting things, naming them, and responding warmly when Irfan points.

qa.q: What is it like for Avni when Irfan checks she is looking?
qa.a: Avni feels happy and connected, laughing because he now shares what he sees with her.

passage:
During Eid, Yusuf's family flat was full of guests. Mehak, one and a half, sat on her father's lap by the balcony.
Yusuf looked up at the paper lanterns and said, "See the moon lantern?" Mehak followed his eyes upward. She stared, then pointed and looked back at him, eyebrows up.
"Yes, the moon!" he said.
Mehak bounced and pointed again, this time at a cousin's shiny bangles. Everyone laughed.

qa.q: What was hanging for Eid?
qa.a: Paper lanterns, including a moon lantern.

qa.q: What does Mehak's raised eyebrows and pointing suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt curious and eager to share what she saw with her father.

qa.q: How could Yusuf support Mehak's pointing?
qa.a: He can name what she points at, look where she looks, and point out new things.

qa.q: How might the guests feel when Mehak points at the bangles?
qa.a: They feel amused and charmed, laughing at her eager sharing.

grounding: Shows a toddler following her father's gaze and pointing to share focus during a festival.

passage:
"Swati, look! Snow!" Vishal said, crouching by the window of the Shimla cottage.
Swati, twenty months, turned toward his voice. He pointed outside. She followed his finger and gasped.
"Snow," he said again.
"No!" she said, which was her word for most things.
She pressed her hand to the cold glass and turned to him, eyes huge.
"Cold!" he laughed.
She pointed at a bird hopping on the white ground, then looked at him.
"Bird, yes!"

qa.q: Where were Swati and Vishal?
qa.a: At the window of the Shimla cottage.

qa.q: How did Swati feel when she saw the snow?
qa.a: She felt amazed and excited, gasping with huge eyes.

qa.q: What is Vishal doing that supports Swati's learning?
qa.a: He points, names what they see together, and answers when she points, sharing her focus.

qa.q: What is it like for Vishal to share Swati's first snow?
qa.a: He feels delighted and warm, laughing and naming things with her.

grounding: Shows a toddler following a pointing gesture and pointing back to share focus in winter.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday morning. Yash, 14 months.
During outdoor time I looked up at a pigeon on the wall and said, "Oh, look!" Yash followed my eyes, found the pigeon, then pointed at it himself and looked back at me, checking that I saw too. His cousin Imran, who is five and was waiting at the gate, laughed and said, "He's showing you!"
Next: I will name what he points at and wait for him to look back.

qa.q: What did Yash find when he followed the teacher's eyes?
qa.a: He found the pigeon on the wall.

qa.q: What does Yash looking back at the teacher suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he was curious and excited, wanting to share the pigeon and check that someone else was enjoying it too.

qa.q: How could Yash's family support this skill at home?
qa.a: They could point to things on walks, name them warmly and wait for Yash to look back, turning each moment into a shared game.
